screens.heading: Inheritance: the is-a relationship
screens.body:
Inheritance lets a new class reuse an existing one. A Dog is an Animal, so Dog extends Animal and automatically gets Animal's fields and methods.

The parent is called the superclass; the child is the subclass. You write the shared stuff once, in the parent, and every child inherits it.
screens.keyPoint: Subclass gets the parent's members for free: code reuse.

check.question: Dog extends Animal. Which methods can a Dog object call?

screens.heading: Overriding and super
screens.body:
A subclass can replace a parent's method with its own version — that's overriding. Mark it with @Override so Java warns you if the signature doesn't match.

Inside the override, super lets you reach the parent's version. And super() as the first line of a constructor calls the parent's constructor.

check.question: What does @Override do for you?
options: Lets the compiler check the method really overrides a parent's
Prevents anyone from calling the method

screens.heading: Polymorphism: many forms
screens.body:
Polymorphism means one interface, many behaviors. Animal pet = new Dog() — the variable is typed Animal, but the object is a Dog.

This is powerful: a method that takes an Animal can accept a Dog, a Cat, or anything new you invent later, without changing the method.
screens.keyPoint: Same call, different behavior depending on the real object.

check.question: Animal pet = new Dog(); pet.speak(); calls…

screens.heading: The call is decided at runtime
screens.body:
With polymorphism, Java looks at the actual object — not the variable type — to pick which method runs. That's called dynamic dispatch.

This happens at runtime, while the program runs. Add new subclasses later and old code automatically works with them.
screens.keyPoint: The real object decides which method runs.

check.question: Dynamic dispatch means the method is chosen…
options: At runtime, based on the actual object
At compile time, based on the variable type

screens.heading: Abstract classes: unfinished blueprints
screens.body:
An abstract class is a parent you can't instantiate — new Animal() is illegal if Animal is abstract. It exists to be extended.

It can mix finished methods with abstract ones (no body). Every concrete subclass must fill in the abstract methods, like filling in the blanks.
screens.keyPoint: Can't instantiate; subclasses complete the blanks.

check.question: What must every concrete subclass of an abstract class do?

screens.heading: Interfaces: pure contracts
screens.body:
An interface is a contract: it lists methods with no bodies, and any class that signs it (with implements) must provide them.

Unlike classes, a class can implement many interfaces. That's how Java gets flexibility without the mess of inheriting from two parents.
screens.keyPoint: A contract of methods; a class can sign many.

check.question: A class can…
options: Implement many interfaces but extend only one class

screens.heading: Abstract class vs interface
screens.body:
Use an abstract class when subclasses share real code and a true 'is-a' bond — Dog and Cat are both Animals. Use an interface when you need a capability across unrelated classes — a Bird and a Plane can both be Flyable.

Quick test: if every implementer would copy-paste the same method body, an abstract class saves that duplication. If the classes have nothing else in common, an interface is cleaner.
screens.keyPoint: Shared code + is-a → abstract class. Shared capability → interface.

check.question: Bird and Airplane both need fly(). Best choice?
